entry.title: Is Anthropic Making Claude Too Human to Control?
entry.content:
Anthropic’s call to slow down AI development to keep humans safe has dominated the news cycle and drew similar calls from the leaders of OpenAI, Microsoft and others (and subtle disagreement from Mark Zuckerberg). 

But Mustafa Suleyman, who runs Microsoft’s AI model development, has a warning about Anthropic itself. 

Suleyman, who co-founded DeepMind (now part of Google), says Anthropic’s approach of treating its Claude models as if they were sentient, similar to humans, could produce a dangerous outcome. He called out Anthropic’s Claude Constitution, a document that treats the model as an intelligent entity and offers guidelines for how it should handle ethical dilemmas. Suleyman said that by incorporating the document into its training, Anthropic could make Claude harder to control. 

Suleyman’s concerns emerged when Anthropic updated the constitution at the start of this year to leave room for the possibility that Claude has some sort of “consciousness” or “moral status,” a change from the original document.

Apple has been developing the server with plans to sell it to AI developers, other businesses and governments, the people said. The product under consideration would come in two versions—a smaller one with two of Apple’s planned M8 Ultra chips clustered together and a bigger one with four M8 Ultra chips. The M-series Ultra chips are Apple’s highest-performance chips and power products including the Mac Studio.

entry.title: Meta Joins Tech’s AI-Fueled Subscription Rush
entry.content:
When it comes to product names, companies tend to move in packs. In video streaming, almost every company included a plus sign in the name brands of their services (Disney+, Paramount+, Apple TV+—you get the picture). In tech, we’ve got Apple One, Google One and now Meta One (we used to have Amazon One, but that has been dropped). Does no one have any imagination? 

Aside from Amazon One, which was a palm-reader system for retail stores, all the other Ones are subscription services for various add-on offerings from the tech firms. Some of these have been around for years—Google One and Apple One have long offered extra amounts of digital storage, along with other perks—but AI is making subscriptions a far more important business model than it has ever been for tech. Google has added extra use of its AI service to its Google One offering. Meta One—unveiled on Tuesday—also offers extra AI usage, as well as some additional tools for using Meta’s social media apps.

entry.title: Anthropic, OpenAI ‘Pacing’ Spooks Some Startup Customers
entry.content:
It’s not clear what impact the pledges by Anthropic and OpenAI to slow the pace of AI development will have on their upcoming public offerings. But the comments are having real effects already: more people outside Silicon Valley and Washington are now alert to potential risks from AI in a way they weren’t even very recently. That’s not great news for startups trying to convince consumers and businesses that the tech is worth it, some investors told me.

One venture capitalist, for example, told me about a startup that has recently found customers to be more wary of buying its AI app for small- and medium-sized businesses in the light of news stories about potentially catastrophic AI.

entry.title: Meta to Launch Camera-Free Smart Glasses Amid Mounting Privacy Concerns
entry.content:
Meta Platforms plans to release a camera-free pair of smart glasses this fall, according to people familiar with the matter, as it looks to expand its hardware lineup amid privacy concerns about cameras on its existing offerings.

The new glasses model, internally code-named Luna, has six built-in microphones that will allow users to speak with Meta’s AI chatbot and its recently launched consumer AI agent, Muse, one of the people said. It also has a button on the side that can be used to quickly activate Meta AI, and speakers like those in its existing models that direct sound toward the user’s ears without covering them. In addition, the glasses have slimmer temple arms than previous Meta smart glasses such as its Ray-Ban models, making them look more like ordinary eyewear.

entry.title: Why Anthropic’s Data Policy Drama Is Good for OpenAI
entry.content:
Major Anthropic customers are still waiting to get “zero data retention” for the newest Fable AI models, meaning the AI firm would not store data related to their usage of its models. In the meantime, some are turning to OpenAI. 

Palantir and Booz Allen, for instance, are expanding their use of OpenAI’s Astra model, which they’ve been able to secure with zero data retention. Both have restricted their use of Fable models because Anthropic said in June it would store customer data for those using Fable models for 30 days, for security reasons.

Before that June announcement, Anthropic offered zero data retention policies in deals negotiated with individual customers. Starting later this fall, the AI firm plans to roll out a new program called Enterprise Frontier Safeguards, which effectively gives “eligible” customers zero data retention.

entry.title: How Erebor Bank’s Sweet Stablecoin Deal Backfired
entry.content:
When Palmer Luckey’s Erebor Bank launched earlier this year, it made an attractive pitch to lure new crypto customers: It would convert their stablecoins to cash for free.

But Erebor wound up pulling the offer after several months, after sophisticated crypto trading firms sniffed out a way to make an easy profit out of the offer—at a cost to Erebor. The episode demonstrates that the young bank is still figuring out how to manage the risks of serving the cryptocurrency industry, a world of fast-moving financial flows, colorful characters and unusual business models.
